## 2.1 Structure Plan

The Structure Plan provides an overview of the intended outcomes for the Punchbowl and Wiley Park Precinct. The Structure Plan has been informed by analysis of the opportunities and constraints of the Village Centres. These opportunities include desired land uses, built form character, housing types, open space, streetscape improvements and pedestrian and cycling connections.

Key elements of the Structure Plan consist of:

- ⚬ Revitalised and vibrant Village Centres with active high streets.
- ⚬ New and enhanced parks and plazas.
- ⚬ New social infrastructure that supports a growing community.
- ⚬ Green connections, shared lanes and pedestrian links that support walking, cycling and social interaction.
- ⚬ Increased tree canopy and green cover to create cool, green and attractive neighbourhoods and to reduce urban heat gain.
- ⚬ High-quality built form outcomes that reflect character of place and protect sensitive interfaces.
- ⚬ The Introduction of creative industries in employment areas.
The Structure Plan is shown in Figure 9.


### Objectives

- O1. To provide an overview of the intended outcomes of the Punchbowl and Wiley Park Precinct.

### Principles

- P1. Development should align with the overarching elements of the Structure Plan as shown in Figure 9.

## 2.2 Character Areas

The Punchbowl and Wiley Park Precinct will be comprised of different areas of distinct character. Through detailed analysis, seven character areas have been identified. Applicants are to identify which character area that a development site is located in and be cognisant of the key attributes of the existing context, where relevant, and the desired future context for the character area.


### Objectives

- O1. To achieve the desired future character of the Punchbowl and Wiley Park Precinct and guide development to deliver this desired character.

### Controls

- C1. Development must consider and address the outcomes expressed in the character area statements and principles.
- C2. Development Applications must be accompanied by a site and context analysis plan that demonstrates an understanding of the manner a site integrates and is consistent with the desired future character area.

### Desired Future Character Areas


### 2.2.1 Punchbowl Village

The Punchbowl Village character area will be a vibrant multi-nodal area which has a focus on the new Metro station. The character area will have an exciting mix of retail, hospitality, community and residential uses with key public open spaces and high streets. A diversity of services will be provided to meet the needs of the community, that includes uses that encourage social interaction. There will be offerings that draw people in and an amenity that encourages them to stay.

Rejuvenated frontages along Breust Place, Punchbowl Road, Highclere Avenue, Arthur Street and The Boulevarde will reinvigorate the Village character area and will be key circulation corridors to and from the Metro Station with new arrival plazas welcoming visitors into the surrounding neighbourhoods.

The architectural character of the Village will respond to the existing 'high street' character of two storey shops with provision of fine-grain retail and human scale street walls encouraging face brick and masonry elements that reflect existing building stock. Street life will be bolstered by improved landscaping and streetscape outcomes. The pre 1950 shop facades will be retained and sympathetically restored.

Adaptive reuse of the heritage-listed former Baby Health Centre and upgraded Rest Park will be a focal point of community life and support the activation of Punchbowl Road.

### 2.2.2 Wiley Park Village

The implementation of the new Metro station and addition population density will inject activity into this character area. The land in this location is comprised of two key sites which will provide housing and active uses at street level.

Wiley Park Village character area will provide a range of retail and other services, as well as being a place that will attract the community to linger. The existing station area will be expanded and will focus retail activation off busy King Georges Road on side streets such as Lakemba Street and Stanlea Parade, where it is quieter with greater amenity. Additional setbacks will assist in re-imaging these as higher quality environments for active uses.

New highrise mixed-use residential developments will be encouraged near the Metro station to concentrate housing, activities and amenities in this highly accessible area.

A continuous and active 4 storey street wall is proposed along King Georges Road, Lakemba Street and Stanlea Parade to provide a consistent built form character. Tower forms are to be set back from the street and be well-separated to ensure good solar access and view sharing. The architectural character will incorporate textured materials such as face brick and timber, reflecting the existing masonry character of Wiley Park.

### 2.2.3 Urban living

The Urban living character areas will be attractive and have high accessibility. These areas will deliver a diversity of higher rise housing, providing a vibrant, safe and desirable street life reinforced by generous soft landscaping and supported by infrastructure.

The area will feature green streets, pedestrian and cycle links, along with inviting public space. This design aims to cultivate a vibrant, walkable urban neighbourhood conveniently located near transport, services and amenity.

The Urban living character area will experience significant renewal with a range of development heights and densities that respond to their context. The greatest densities will be delivered in proximity to Metro stations and services and on those sites which are larger in area and orientated to achieve high quality development outcomes.

New developments will prioritise direct street access and landscaped private open space within setbacks for ground-floor apartments and terraces, encouraging passive surveillance of the streets, pedestrian links and shared lanes. Apartments adjacent to open space will be designed to provide a high quality interface and frontage to parks.

Podiums and rooftops will offer opportunities to contribute to urban greening and communal open space for residents.

Parts of this character area contain existing residential flat buildings while others include detached dwellings. New development will need to be sensitive to both contexts, providing appropriate setbacks, landscaping and articulated built form.

#### Principles

- P1. New taller developments must be sympathetic to the surrounding context, which includes detached dwellings, threestorey walk-ups and newer apartment buildings. In areas interfacing with lowerdensity zones, a sensitive transition is essential. This should be achieved through careful consideration of scale, setbacks, separation, landscaping, and privacy measures. See Section 4.2 The building envelope.

- P5. Slender, elegant towers set upon podiums will exhibit high quality design of form that responds to context including the orientation of facades. Longer podiums will include articulation to ensure they do not overwhelm the streetscape and provide visual interest. High quality materials and finishes should be used at the interface with the public domain. See Section 4.2.1 Building height and storeys and 4.4 Visual diversity, articulation and fine grain.
- P6. The use of brick and masonry, along with exposed concrete structure in podiums, will reflect the existing brick materiality of the character area, ensuring cohesion with the surrounding architectural context. See Section 4.5 Materials and finishes.
- P2. Development adjacent to public open space, including Wiley Park, will be orientated to face the park and provide passive surveillance through the implementation of entrances, balconies and terraces.
- P3. High quality pedestrian links must be free of obstructions and feature landscaping along their edges. These links should also include adequate lighting as well as apartments with direct entries from the public domain to increase activity and enhance passive surveillance. See Section 4.3.1 Residential ground floor.
- P4. Encourage the provision of small scale retail, commercial, food and drink premises, where permissible, at street corners and through site links to create active edges. See Section 4.3.2 Active street frontages and edges.

### 2.2.5 Low-rise living

This character area is generally located at the periphery of the Village Centres and will accommodate moderate renewal. New development will include single dwellings, dual occupancies, terraces/ townhouses and multi-dwelling housing. The existing quiet residential character will be retained. 15.0 15.0 6.0 12.0

The existing low scale character of these areas will be celebrated and new development will be sympathetic to the existing scale. The streetscape will be enhance through increased landscaping and tree canopy within front setbacks. Driveway crossovers will be minimised where possible.

New development will draw upon the form and materiality of existing dwellings including the pattern of pitched roofs, generally facebrick and masonry walls and landscape character. Existing tree planting will be maintained and supplemented with additional canopy cover.

Developments are to demonstrate a range of residential building types that consist of one to two storeys and include single dwellings, dual occupancies, terraces, townhouses, multi-dwelling housing and low-scale apartments. Create an inviting street edge and preserve the landscape character of the area See Section 4.1 Minimum lot sizes and Section 4.2.1 Building height and storeys.
- P3. Maintain and draw inspiration from the surrounding design and materials of existing homes, reflecting the patterns, setbacks, pitched roofs, dark brick and masonry structures, quality finishes and maintain the bulk and scale with the surrounding architectural context to create cohesion throughout See Section 4.5 Materials and finishes.

## 2.3 Connecting with Country


### Objectives

- O1. To recognise, respect and respond to Aboriginal cultural heritage in the planning, development and daily life of Punchbowl and Wiley Park Precinct.

### Principles

- P1. To take a Country centred approach and thinking that is layered into new development in the Precinct and is consistent with the Government Architect NSW 'Connecting with Country framework' (CWCF).
- P2. To integrate Aboriginal cultural practices, history, narratives, and values in the design of proposed development.
- P3. To encourage development to respond to the physical and cultural connection of the local Aboriginal community to the land.
- P4. Foster collaboration and knowledge sharing between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal individuals.

### Controls

- C1. For development where clause 6.15 of the Canterbury-Bankstown Local Environmental Plan 2023 applies, the development must demonstrate:
- How the design considers aspects of Country under Sections 3 and 4 of the Government Architect NSW CWCF;
- How the design gives regard to the culture and heritage of the traditional custodians of the land, the Darug People, on which the development is proposed, including;
- Connecting design with the existing site topography, natural environment and landscape setting; and
- Incorporating sustainable practices by using natural building materials.

<!-- SRC: 7-7-punchbowl-and-wiley-park.pdf | PAGE: 34 -->

![page 34 img 1 (301x632)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0034-86c4d3616e2b.png)

- C2. For development where Design Excellence clause of the Canterbury-Bankstown Local Environmental Plan 2023 applies, the development must determine the appropriate scope of engagement with the Aboriginal community and its representatives, whether it be high, medium or low as outlined in Section 3.1 of the Government Architect NSW CWCF. If engaging with the Aboriginal community, development must:
- Demonstrate the methods and outcomes from engagement with the Aboriginal community; and
- Adhere to protocols outlined in the NSW Government's Practice Note 'Engaging with Aboriginal Communities' and 'Aboriginal Cultural and Intellectual Property Protocol'.
- C3. If significant items such as ancestral remains or artefacts are discovered during subsoil investigations, excavation, demolition or other earthworks, the applicant must engage with the Aboriginal community to determine culturally appropriate handling, repatriation or reburial.
- C4. Development that proposes open space and landscaping should demonstrate consideration of 'walking Country' which reflects Aboriginal cultural practices, artefacts, artwork and narratives. Aspects involving the senses of seeing, hearing, touching, smelling and tasting, should be included.
Image - NAIDOC Family Day 2023 (Source: Canterbury-Bankstown Council)

- C5. Design aspects of each development should give regard to the culture and heritage of the traditional custodians of the land, the Darug People, on which the development is proposed. The following design opportunities should be considered to ensure a Country-centred approach:
- Connect design with the natural environment and landscape setting, being: people, animals, resources and plants equally.
- Acknowledge shared history between Aboriginal and colonial settlers to promote healing and reconciliation by incorporating storytelling and knowledge of the past.
- Incorporate sustainable practices by using natural building materials that have a cultural and heritage significance.
- Incorporate Aboriginal place names, as guided by the Geographic Names Board, to foster understanding and raise awareness.
- Focus on details and patterns to insert cultural meaning.
- C6. All work prepared is to address the Connecting with Country objectives, principles and controls and must address the NSW Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property Protocol, to ensure applicants are aware of their duties with respect to the integration of this content.

## 3.1 Public domain strategy

The public domain consists of streets, squares, parks, shared lanes and pedestrian links. These elements, in conjunction with the built form interface on private land, play a vital role in creating unique, vibrant and sustainable places that are attractive, inviting and inclusive for all.

The public domain strategy ensures housing growth is supported by the delivery of high-quality public spaces that encourage walking, cycling, community interaction, and engagement.

This section outlines key opportunities for enhancing the public domain in the Punchbowl and Wiley Park Precinct, as identified in Figure 21. Public Domain Strategy.


### Objectives

- O1. To improve the quality, appearance and function of the public domain.
- O2. Provide a diverse range of quality public spaces to support residents, workers and visitors.
- O3. Ensure a high level of permeability and accessibility throughout Precinct.
- O4. Provide high quality, functional and attractive formal and informal spaces for community interaction.
- O5. To establish a vibrant and attractive Precinct where the network of streets, shared lanes and open spaces support the increase in population density, the increased pedestrian movement and footpath trading activities.
- Variety of public spaces to meet the needs of the community 1
- Permeable connected network that encourages walking, cycling and public transport use 2
- Tree canopy and shade, surveillance of the 4
- landscaping for cool, attractive places that promote biodiversity 3

## 3.2 Public open space and publicly accessible open space

Public open spaces are provided on public land whereas publicly accessible spaces are located on private land and can be accessed by the public. Both spaces comprise parks and plazas with green open space and/or hardscaped spaces and high quality landscaping.


### Objectives

- O1. To ensure that the size, type, accessibility and program of open spaces accommodates the future number of residents, workers and visitors and their recreational and passive needs throughout the day and night.
- O2. To create new connections to open space to ensure easy, convenient access by walking and cycling to existing and proposed open space.
- O3. To provide new open space and publicly accessible open space in under-served areas and upgrade existing open space.
- O4. Ensure that any proposed privately owned publicly accessible space have a full public nature equivalent to the public domain.
- O5. To ensure development contributes to a diverse network of quality and attractive open spaces comprised of well-connected parks and squares, green streets and lanes.
- O6. To ensure open space has a high level of solar access and shade that is suitable to purpose.
Image - Bulleke-bek Park, adjacent to Nightingale ParkLife development, Brunswick, VIC (Source: Architectus)

![page 39 img 1 (734x796)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0039-106ad7e88e92.png)


<!-- SRC: 7-7-punchbowl-and-wiley-park.pdf | PAGE: 40 -->


### Principles

- P1. Provide equitable access and a variety of amenity and recreational options to accommodate different community needs.
- P2. The design of new publicly accessible open space and public open space should use a palette of high quality and robust materials to maximise design lifespan and create beautiful places. Landscaping treatments and material selections must respond to the local character of each space and contribute to a cohesive and unified public domain throughout the Precinct.
- P3. Create and enhance natural ecologies within the urban fabric through the use of diverse native landscape species.
- P4. Paths of travel through public open space must respond to 'desire paths' and should be lit in the evening to improve safety and accessibility for users.
- P5. In high activity area where street space and footpaths are constrained, create a suitable environment for pedestrian movement and business activity by widening existing footpaths into private land.
- A Country centred approach should be taken to the design of open space. See Section 2.3 Connecting with Country.
- Consideration must be given to the reduction of urban heat and the provision of shade in the design of open space. See Section 3.6 Shade and the reduction of urban heat.

### Controls

- C1. Where required by Council, new publicly accessible space and/or land dedication for new or expanded public open space must be provided in the locations identified in Figure 21 Public Domain Strategy.
- C2. Development fronting open space must engage with these publicly accessible spaces. This can be achieved by, but is not limited to, the following:
- ⚬ Ground level active frontages and edges.
- ⚬ Balconies addressing open space.
- ⚬ Garden apartments with individual entries from the open space.
- ⚬ Access from development sites and lanes to and from open space.
- C3. Buildings and building basements are not permitted to be located on, above or under any proposed new open space. Awnings can overhang open space.
- C4. Public art must be integrated into publicly accessible open spaces.This could include a Connection with Country approach. The design and placement of public art must contribute meaningfully to the character, identity and activation of the public domain.

## 3.3 Streets, shared lanes, pedestrian links and arcades

Streets, shared lanes and pedestrian links are places of movement : to watch, to pass through and see the movement of people. This public framework provides for social and commercial exchange.

In urban areas, a well-designed network of shared lanes and pedestrian links are essential for improving permeability and connecting to main streets and open space, creating walkability and equity of access and enjoyment.

The street should be safe and inviting to pedestrians and cyclists while accommodating vehicles and traffic and be enhanced by tree canopies that promote amenity and sustainability.

Pedestrian links prioritise pedestrians and cyclists, featuring open skies and awnings, while shared lanes also accommodate service vehicles and driveway access.

Arcades serve as internal retail 'lanes' that enhance permeability and provide an engaging shopping experience. These narrow, intimate spaces encourage pedestrians to come and stay and facilitate connections through street blocks, reducing walking distances.

New development is essential for contributing to a high-quality, permeable, and connected movement network that is green, inviting and safe for everyone. This is achieved by thoughtfully designing how a development interfaces with streets, lanes and pedestrian links. Setbacks, public domain improvements and new connections should be considered.

Image - Visualisation of tree lined street with cycleway in Bankstown City Centre (Source: Canterbury-Bankstown Council)

![page 41 img 1 (735x797)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0041-76b2c9645588.png)

### Objectives

- O1. To improve connectivity for pedestrians and cyclists between key destination points.
- O2. To provide a high quality, safe, connected cycle network that enables the community to choose to ride to work, home or a destination.
- O3. To ensure shared lanes, pedestrian links and arcades are accessible, attractive, continuous, well-lit, safe and where appropriate, open to the sky.
- O4. To provide amenity and safety to existing and proposed shared lanes, pedestrian links and arcades and active uses to engage pedestrians, where appropriate.
Image - Pedestrian link with landscaping and garden apartments, Zetland (Source: Architectus)


### Principles

- P1. Large development sites and sites located in the middle of large blocks should provide pedestrian links to improve permeability.
- P2. Development must incorporate design measures that enhance pedestrian safety and comfort, including passive surveillance from habitable rooms and private open space, well-lit pathways and clear sightlines.
- P3. Development that interfaces with pedestrian links should consider providing an active edge, where possible.
- O5. To design shared lanes, pedestrian links and arcades that provide an intimate space to linger within a fine grain spatial network.
- O6. To provide for vehicular entries and servicing away from primary street frontages using shared lanes.

### Controls

- C1. Where required by Council, shared lanes, pedestrian links and arcades must be provided in the locations identified in Figure 21 Public Domain Strategy. These connections must be designed to ensure for permeability, safety and integration with the broader movement network.
- C2. Figures 22 to 28 illustrate cross-sections of Council's vision for specific streets, lanes and pedestrian links in the Punchbowl and Wiley Park Precinct. Development in these areas must demonstrate how the built form, setback treatments and any public domain improvements align with and contribute to delivering this vision.
Image - Activated pedestrian link, Surry Hills Village, Redfern (Source: Architectus)

- C3. Pedestrian links are to have a minimum width of 4m and cater for the movement of pedestrians and cyclists in both directions. Shared lanes are to have a minimum width of 9m. These key public domain assets are to be designed to:
- Ensure that buildings or structures are not located over any proposed pedestrian link, other than awnings.
- Provide lighting, paving, street furniture and tree planting to clearly indicate the priority of the pedestrian or cycling user, (to be provided in accordance with Council's specifications and design standards).
- Development must demonstrate the provision of physical and visual connections with neighbouring sites, including any
necessary level adjustments. Detailed plans illustrating these connections are to be provided as part of the Development Application.

- Awnings should be provided for active frontages and active edges for weather protection, offering shade and shelter from sun and rain. Awnings are to be designed and delivered in accordance with the requirements specified in Section 4.3.2 Active street frontages and edges.
- Stormwater management measures must be incorporated to minimise the flow of pollutants from shared lanes and pedestrian links. Treatments must be implemented in accordance with Section 3 - Stormwater Drainage Systems of the CBDCP 2023.

- Shared lanes and pedestrian links should be clear of all obstructions, including stairs, escalators and columns and provide a clear line of sight from one end to the other for surveillance and accessibility.
- Shared lanes and pedestrian links will be open 24 hours a day, well-lit and adhere to Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) principles.
- Where a development has the potential to create a shared lane or pedestrian link by extending an existing or proposed lane within its site, the lane should be completed or extended within the development site. If a development can deliver part of a lane or initiate a new lane, it should make provision for it.
- C9. Pedestrian links and new shared lanes are to be registered as an easement on title or dedicated to Council prior to issue of an Occupation Certificate. Council reserves the right to not accept dedication. Any proposed dedication must be discussed at a pre-lodgement meeting.
- C10. The maintenance of the shared lane and pedestrian link in perpetuity including cleaning, repairing and replacing damaged or worn paving, furniture and the like and maintaining landscaping in a healthy condition is the responsibility of the land owner, not Council. A management plan must accompany any development involving the provision of a shared lane or pedestrian
Image - Enhanced shared lane with street art, activation and bike parking, Rose Street, Fitzroy (Source: Architectus)

link. The plan is to demonstrate how ongoing access, maintenance, and functionality of the shared lane or pedestrian link will be ensured, including through any future changes in ownership.

- C11. Arcades within retail and commercial developments are to be designed to:
- Be two storeys in height or where proposed as a single storey at ground level, have a minimum floor to ceiling height of 5m.
- Have widths of 4m - 6m where the links are provided within a two storey height, or 5m - 8m wide where provided at a single floor level.
- Be located at ground level and lined with spaces to facilitate active uses.
- Be designed to have access to natural light.
- Be open at each end, or where air conditioned, provide entry doors that are glazed and comprise a minimum 70% of the width of the entrance.
- Be publicly accessible from 6am to 10pm each day.

## 3.4 Tree canopy, green cover and deep soil

Trees are essential for their contribution to the amenity and character of the Precinct. When appropriately selected, located, planted and maintained, trees provide a multitude of benefits to the urban environment including reducing heat gain, providing shade and mitigating climate change.

One of the most effective solutions to mitigate urban heat gain is expanding tree canopy cover. Trees provide shade, cool the environment through transpiration and reduce surface temperature in densely built areas, where heat can become trapped by concrete and asphalt. Temperature differences between locations with canopy and without canopy gaps can be significant.

Greencover provides further greening and shade to buildings and to the site itself. This will protect buildings from radiant heat gain and provide a pleasing aesthetic to the public domain.

Deep soil is 'landscaped area'. These areas of soil are not covered by buildings or structures. Deep soil provides for the planting of canopy trees, increases water filtration and reduces stormwater runoff. It is beneficial to co-locate deep soil with communal open space to provide shade and amenity for those using these spaces.

Image - Markham Avenue, Ashburton, VIC, Architectus (Source: Architectus)


### Objectives

- O1. To provide tree canopy for shade to maximise amenity to public space during the periods of the day they are most used for recreation or repose.
- O2. To improve and enhance environmental biodiversity and mitigate heat at ground level.
- O3. To ensure for maximum tree canopy in development on private land and public land.
- O4. To create a continuous tree canopy, mitigate climate change and to improve the health and wellbeing of people and ecosystems.
- O5. To provide green cover to soften building form, create amenity for occupants and provide for a green aesthetic to the public domain.
- O6. To maximise canopy coverage by bundling or undergrounding aerial power cables.
- O7. To provide deep soil to increase tree canopy, landscape, water infiltration and the reduction of stormwater runoff.
![page 52 img 1 (885x981)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0052-27c8f31676a0.png)


<!-- SRC: 7-7-punchbowl-and-wiley-park.pdf | PAGE: 53 -->


### Principles

- P1. Ensure existing trees are protected and that additional trees are planted in the public and private domains.
- P2. Provide tree planting appropriate to the local climate.
- P3. Provide for recreational equipment, seating, landscaping, absorptive ground treatments and an integrated consistent material palette for hard landscaped areas.
- P4. Ensure for adequate deep soil depth and width for the growth of large trees, shrubs and vegetation generally.
- P5. In new development ensure for articulated facades for green cover. In alterations to existing buildings, provide fixed planting and rooftop greenery.

### Controls

- C1. As part of a Development Application for residential, mixed use or non-residential development, street trees are to be provided to all public frontages to the satisfaction of Council.
- C2. New street trees must have a minimum pot size of 75 litres but no greater than 200 litres.
- C3. Street trees should be planted with clearances as set out in Table 1.
- C4. A Public Frontage Plan(PFP) shall be prepared prior to the issue of a Construction Certificate. This plan will identify:
- All frontages of the development site
between the gutter and the building line, including the footpath, drainage, entries and other built objects.

- Any existing trees, bus shelters, signage and other structures or services that may impede the planting of new street trees.
- A qualified landscape architect shall prepare the PFP and specify the size in litres, the spacing and species in coordination with Council. The PFP must be prepared after test pits have been completed to ensure for services coordination
- C5. Trees will be spaced depending on their size: small - 5-7m, medium 7-10m and large 10-15m.
- C6. Please refer to tree base treatments in the Appendices
- C7. Minimum tree canopy cover is required on private land as per Table 2 and Figure 29.
- C8. Tree canopy cover refers to the layer of leaves, branches, and stems of trees that cover the ground when viewed from above, expressed as proportion of the total site area, calculated in accordance with the following:
- Canopy area is to include the expected mature size, (crown spread at maturity), of existing and proposed trees.
- Only trees with a minimum crown spread of 3m in diameter are to be included. Trees with a crown spread less than 3m diameter are to be excluded from tree canopy cover calculations.
- Any overlap in canopy area is to be counted once.
- Canopy area extending outside of site boundaries is to be excluded.
- Canopy area extending within a development site from trees planted in adjoining sites is to be excluded.
- Trees located over structures, including podiums and rooftops, are to be included.
- C9. The design of the canopy trees should be laid out such that sufficient room is provided for the trees to achieve their desired mature size. Canopy overlap should not exceed 25%.
- C10. New development within the E1 Local Centre zone, must deliver 50% of the site area as 'green cover' which can be any combination of the following:
- ⚬ Deep soil zones;
- ⚬ Green walls where orientation is appropriate;
- ⚬ Layered planting on structure (including small and medium trees, as per the Apartment Design Guide);
- ⚬ Green roofs and awnings; or
- ⚬ Permanent planting on balconies and podiums, (including built-in planter boxes).

## 3.5 Solar access to open space


### Objectives

- O1. To ensure for solar access to parks and spaces for the enjoyment of residents and visitors.
- O2. To balance sunlight access to the principal useable parts of public open space with shaded areas to enable a range of activities and the planting of a variety of trees and vegetation.
- O3. To maintain or maximise solar access to public space during periods of the day when they are most used.
- O4. To ensure the successful growth and survival of trees and vegetation within parks and public spaces.

### Principles

- P1. Provide high levels of solar access to ensure that trees and vegetation thrive and amenity is provided for the community.
- P2. Provide solar access on balance with shaded areas to ensure for amenity to all users all year around.
- P3. Ensure that access to winter sun is maximised.
Image - 1 Central Courtyard, Macquarie University, NSW (Source: Architectus)


### Controls

- C1. Development Applications must demonstrate that the hours of solar access outlined in Figure 30 are maintained or preferably exceeded.
- C2. Where overshadowing of parks and spaces is likely, a statement with supporting solar access studies must be submitted by a registered architect demonstrating that the proposed development mitigates overshadowing to the affected open space or publicly accessible space.
- C3. Ancillary structures such as columns, pillars, spires, flag poles, public art, and architectural roof features including equipment for servicing the building, such as plant, lift motor rooms, fire stairs and the like, must not be excluded from any overshadowing analysis.

## 3.6 Shade and the reduction of urban heat

Punchbowl and Wiley Park face a significant urban heat island effect due to climate change and low tree canopy cover. The combination of roads, infrastructure and buildings with limited greenery leads to increased heat absorption, raising summer temperatures to over 30.5 degrees Celsius, and even reaching 45.9 degrees in the past. Australia has one of the highest rates of skin cancer globally.

Shade, provided by natural elements or structures, is essential for comfort, UV protection and to encouraging social activity. When combined with water features, permeable paving and appropriate materials, shade can effectively reduce heat gain. Together, shade and seating while balancing solar access foster healthy, vibrant, attractive communities.

Image - Umbrellas and trees provide shading of playground at North Rosebery Park, Rosebery, NSW (Source: Architectus)


### Objectives

- O1. To ensure for refuge from hot summer sun in public and publicly accessible open space.
- O2. To create imaginative responses for shade that integrate with playgrounds, water features and areas for the community to congregate in.
- O3. To ensure for high amenity public and private spaces that are pleasurable to use.
- O4. To reduce the contribution of new development to the urban heat island effect by retaining and providing design elements that store water, minimising impermeable surfaces to increase rainwater infiltration and allow for the improved cooling effects of evaporation.
- O5. To ensure the location of tree planting and vegetation has considered the location of where people sit and children play to provide shade and reduce radiant heat.
- O6. To improve user comfort in public domain and space accessible to the public.

<!-- SRC: 7-7-punchbowl-and-wiley-park.pdf | PAGE: 58 -->

![page 58 img 1 (334x582)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0058-6a52ece120a2.png)


### Principles

- P1. Create shade linkages through implementing shade structures, awnings to shop fronts and planting trees.
- P2. Integrate water features such as misting, sprays and water fountains and the like where shade is provided in public and publicly accessible open space.
- P3. Consider the location of trees and structures and the resultant shadow that will be created. Locate seating and areas where people can rest in these shaded areas.
- P4. Maximise greenery throughout the Precinct to reduce urban heat.
- P5. Shade paved surfaces and walls where possible but also consider solar access in winter months.
![page 58 img 2 (326x582)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0058-37cf5af8cb90.png)


*Dr Darragh Park, Mascot, NSW (Source: Architectus)*


*Darling Square, Haymarket, NSW (Source: Architectus)*

![page 59 img 1 (289x218)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0059-ebc56d4af551.png)


### Controls

- C1. Retain existing trees to maintain shade.
- C2. Use deciduous trees in public open spaces to provide shade in summer and sun in winter.
- C3. Improve cooling by locating trees to provide shade to exposed building walls, hard surfaces and pedestrian walkways.
- C4. Use trees and shade structures in combination with water features to reduce temperatures in public open space and publicly accessible spaces.
- C5. Store water in the landscape using fountains and water play features and the like.
- C6. If a dark roof is used, green cover must cover the roof form. Consider reflectivity in the choice of roof material and the colour.
- C7. Minimise the reflection of solar heat from facades by selecting appropriate materials.
- C8. Ensure that play equipment is shaded to increase useability.

## 4.1 Minimum lot sizes

A minimum lot size for certain residential dwelling types is required to ensure lots are large enough to accommodate the development. This particularly applies to residential flat buildings to ensure that adequate frontage and amenity are provided.


### Objectives

- O1. Ensure lots are large enough to accommodate required setbacks and separation to adjoining properties, including ground floor outdoor uses such as private open space and landscaped areas, driveways, play areas, pedestrian access, set down and pick up areas, carparks and vehicle manoeuvring areas.
- O2. Minimise adverse impacts of development on the amenity of the area.
- O3. Require lot amalgamation to achieve minimum lot frontage and size requirements.
- O4. Ensure lots are large enough to protect special attributes, including natural or cultural features, heritage items, heritage conservation areas, trees and natural topographical features.
- O5. Prevent fragmentation or isolation of land.

### Controls

- C1. Development within the Precinct, as identified in Figure 3. Land Application Map, must comply with minimum lot size and lot frontage as required in the CBLEP 2023.

## 4.2 The building envelope


### 4.2.1 Building heights and storeys

The maximum building heights in the Precinct are stipulated in the CBLEP 2023. This section of the DCP provides further guidance on the bulk, scale and design of buildings, ensuring for careful consideration of impacts on streets, shared lanes, open space and pedestrian links.


#### Objectives

- O1. To design taller buildings that allow for adequate provision of sunlight to streets and open space for pedestrian amenity and to allow trees to grow.
- O2. To design a distinctive and legible skyline to identify the Village Centres and Metro stations.
- O3. To ensure buildings are designed in consideration of wind impacts to the public domain.
- O4. To design elegant slender towers that have consideration for view sharing.
- O5. To ensure taller buildings express a strong architectural response defined by a clearly identified concept or idea to create a sense of place.
- O6. To provide for landmark towers on prominent corners to improve the legibility of the Precinct.
- Slender, elegant towers well separated 1
- Height and scale responds to character and context 2

#### Principles

- P1. Concentrate taller buildings around the Metro stations and civic areas to maximise housing provision in well located areas.
- P2. Ensure that towers over 4 or 5 storeys are setback above a podium to mitigate bulk and dominance of the street.
- P3. Ensure the height and scale of new developments are site specific and developed in response to key features of the site and setting.
- P4. Manage wind conditions promote outdoor planting, including green roofs, green cover and other landscaping elements as well as tables, chairs and other furniture used by building occupants on balconies and outdoor areas on buildings.
Image - Tall brick tower, Zetland, NSW, CO-AP (Source: Architectus)


#### Controls

- C1. A wind impact assessment is required for:
- Buildings over 25m in height.
- Buildings without a podium on a corner sites.
- C2. Buildings without a podium are permitted on corner sites. In cases where a podium is not proposed, the building is to:
- Be designed to mitigate down drafts to the public domain in accordance with a Wind Impact Assessment report;
- Be designed 'in the round' (i.e. consideration of the design quality when being viewed from within the Precinct, from the street level, from within other buildings, from the street and from a distance); and
- Provide a high quality ground plane for pedestrians at street level.
- C3. Development must not exceed the number of storeys shown for the site on Figure 34. Maximum building height in storeys map.

### 4.2.3 Street wall

Together with the public domain, the street wall with active street frontage is the built element that shapes the way most of the city is experienced.

The street wall provides spatial enclosure and must operate in concert with other street walls or podiums to form a satisfying and rich experience of the public spaces of the city or place for the community. Interruptions or erosions of the street wall generally work to undermine the vitality and definition of the street wall and are not favoured.


#### Objectives

- O1. To ensure that the visual relationship between the street and public space is reinforced.
- O2. To design the street wall to achieve fine grain modulation to create visual interest and variety while ensuring for consistency in streetscape character.
- O3. To create a vertical rhythm and visual interest to reduce the scale of building mass.
- O4. To implement an articulation zone within podiums and facades to allow architectural form to develop.
1

that responds to its context

- Define the space and interface with the street and public spaces 2
Provide an articulation zone modulation and vertical rhythm 3

#### Principles

- P1. Street wall design should reflect the context and interface with a particular street typology as set out in Section 3.
- P2. Design the street wall to provide an appropriate human scale, material quality and detail.
- P3. Minimise large expanses of inactive frontage.
- P4. Retain and sensitively integrate existing heritage and historic pre 1950 shopfronts into new development.

#### Controls

- C1. Street wall heights must be consistent with Figure 38. For Council to consider a variation to a street wall height it must be demonstrated by the following:
- A street wall elevation at 1:500 scale in context showing existing buildings on the same block with consideration given to the proposed heights; and
- A detailed street wall elevation at 1:200 scale that includes the buildings immediately adjacent.

*Figure 5. Elevation showing how new development is seamlessly integrated into the existing street wall*

- C2. Where a street frontage length of an individual building exceeds 45m in length, it is to appear broken into two or more buildings each with different architectural characters. This outcome could be achieved through the following articulation design considerations or through other alternative design considerations to the reasonable satisfaction of Council:
- Vertical elements must be separated by indentations at a scale legible in the street and use a varied architectural expression and materiality.
- In cases where there is a range of heights in a street wall, prioritise the lower range along laneways, pedestrian links, and areas with high pedestrian activity.
- C3. Existing pre-1950 historic shopfront street walls in civic streets are to be sensitively integrated into new development.
- C4. Where the adjacent built form context is of a lower scale and not anticipated to change, development must provide a transition to the lower scaled built form and include appropriate articulation to fit with the context.
- C5. For sites including or adjacent to heritage items, development must transition in scale and height and provide adequate separation and appropriate articulation to respect the established scale of the heritage item or context.
- C6. Datums derived from listed heritage buildings on the site or on an adjoining property - that is, the heights of the main ridgelines (or parapets in the case of commercial buildings), top plates/eaves level (or awnings of commercial buildings) and ground floor levels (street or natural ground levels)-must be used to ensure composition of height and scale is visually harmonious.

### 4.2.5 Upper storey setbacks


#### Objectives

- O1. To ensure buildings are setback above street walls to reinforce the scale of streets, mitigate wind down drafts to pedestrians and dominance of the public domain.
- O2. To ensure that upper storey setbacks allow for the enjoyment of sun and daylight within public spaces, provide for views of the sky and allow trees to grow.
- O3. To provide for appropriate transition and sympathetic response to lower-scaled buildings and significant elements within the local context.
- O4. To create opportunities for tree canopy, planting and outdoor open space on podiums.

- P1. Clearly delineate the street wall by using upper storey setbacks and create a visual break in tall building facades.
- P2. Encourage green cover and useable spaces on podiums and rooftops.
- P3. Promote generous commercial, communal and residential balconies on upper storey setbacks.
- P4. The taller portion of the building is setback above a podium to ensure the bulk and scale is sympathetic to existing and future development and to streets. This mitigates dominance to pedestrians at street level.

### 4.2.6 Building separation


#### Objectives

- O1. To ensure sunlight penetrates through to street level to protect the amenity of pedestrians and allow street trees to grow.
- O2. To ensure that taller buildings are not overwhelming and overcrowded and appear as distinct elements within the skyline with space around them.
- O3. To provide adequate privacy, access to light, air and outlook to the sky for the occupants of buildings, neighbouring properties and future buildings.
- O4. To ensure development does not unfairly limit the re-development potential of adjoining sites in the future.

#### Principles

- P1. Building design should avoid using multiple upper-level setback 'steps' that result in a 'wedding cake' or a 'ziggurat' appearance.
- P2. Maintain adequate separation distances between buildings on the same site to protect access to sunlight and sky views and improve air circulation between buildings.
- P3. Provide separation to enable a building to be seen from all sides and to allow for articulation that responds to orientation.

### 4.2.7 Maximum floorplate area


#### Objectives

- O1. To ensure towers are not bulky, provide good amenity to building occupants and appear slender, elegant and well-proportioned when view from streets and from distance.
- O2. To allow for views to the sky from streets and lanes.
- O3. To reduce building bulk and minimise its impact on streets, public spaces, and street trees by mitigating adverse effects such as overshadowing and urban heat gain.
- O4. To ensure floor plates are limited to a certain area and configuration in accordance with use.

#### Principles

- P1. Shallow floorplates and glazing to southern facades are favourable for providing excellent natural daylight.
- P2. Achieve living and working environments with good internal amenity and minimise the need for artificial cooling and heating.

## 4.3 Building interface


### Objectives 4.3.1 Residential ground floor

- O1. To establish new canopy trees within setbacks that contribute to the character of the street and provide residents amenity and privacy.
- O2. To provide ownership and identity to residents by providing individual entries along the ground floor frontage out to the public domain.
- O3. To provide for surveillance of public and publicly accessible space.
- O4. To encourage detailed attention to the design and to selection of materials at the lower level of residential buildings.

### Principles

- P1. Provide individual courtyards to ground floor apartments.
- P2. Existing and proposed tree canopy should be contained within front setbacks to provide residents amenity and privacy and to offer greenery to the public domain.

### Controls

- C1. A minimum of 3 metres depth of deep soil shall be allocated from the front boundary. Canopy trees must be planted in this area 2 metres away from the front building line to achieve at least 8 metres mature height and spread, at the rate of 1 canopy tree for every 8 lineal metres of frontage. The number of trees to be planted will be rounded up to the next whole number.
- C2. The first tree will be planted at the intersection of the front and side boundary. The medium to large sized trees will be spaced and planted from this origin point.
- C3. All ground floor apartments shall have individual entries and individual courtyard for private open space.

### 4.3.2 Active street frontages and edges

Active street frontages are continuous retail and business uses with frequent openings that engage with the street and public space, creating a lively, welcoming environment that encourages pedestrian activity. To create a human and scale,' active street frontages should feature a fine grain of narrow shopfronts with services and utilities positioned away from the primary frontage.

Active edges are incidental active uses along a frontage. While secondary to active street frontages, they contribute positively to the public domain. For example, Canterbury Road would primarily includes business uses that will have less foot traffic but still provide occasional active use to service workers and pedestrians along this street. In residential areas, an active edge could include a café or corner shop, on a lane, pedestrian link or open space, with the remainder of the ground floor frontage being garden apartments with individual entries.

Active uses typically include retail, customer service areas, cafes, restaurants and outdoor dining areas.

To enhance the pedestrian comfort and encourage street life, active street frontages must incorporate continuous awnings. Awnings should also be provided along active edges, where possible, although they do not need to extend along the entire length of the frontage.

Image - Active frontages along sharedway at Marrickville Metro, Marrickville, NSW (Source: Architectus)

#### Objectives

- O1. To encourage finer grained narrow frontages with a high standard of design to create varied experiences that provide views into and out of shops.
- O2. To ensure that Punchbowl Road, The Boulevarde and Lakemba Street have a high quality and engaging public realm.
- O3. To ensure that the interface and amenity of Canterbury Road is improved for pedestrians.
- O4. To ensure frontages along key streets, pedestrian links, lanes and open spaces provide both active and passive surveillance.
- O5. To encourage people to linger and enjoy public space.
- O6. To ensure that building services do not dominate the pedestrian experience and are designed as an integrated part of the building form.
- O7. To create opportunities to enjoy the positive aspects of climate and shield people from the negative such as wind, rain and heat.
- O8. To provide secondary active edges that create vitality and interest on frontages with less foot traffic.

#### Principles

- P1. Vehicle entries are located away from key pedestrian areas.
- P2. Awnings are to be used along active street frontages and edges to provide comfort and amenity.
- P3. Shopfronts utilise lighting in the evenings when people are using public space for safety and activation.

- C1. The location of active street frontages and active edges are shown on Figure 47 .
- C2. Vehicle access and loading is to be located away from primary pedestrian areas.
- C3. Extend the concrete structural frame to form the awning at street level to shield pedestrians on active street frontages.
- C4. Awnings are to be provided to active street frontages and extend 3m over the footway to provide protection from inclement weather and hot sun. Awnings must:
- Integrate with the built form;
- Not be double height;
- Be non-reflective and not glazed; and
- Be harmonious with adjacent awnings and gutters and integrate downpipes and lighting.
- C5. Awning should be provided to active edges where ever possible.

## 4.4 Visual diversity, articulation and fine grain


### Objectives

- O1. Encourage variety in architectural design and character to provide a fine grain which enriches and enlivens the Precinct's public domain.
- O2. Ensure building mass is reduced by articulating building envelopes into smaller components.
- O3. Ensure that the scale, modulation and façade articulation of development responds to the character within the Precinct.
- O4. To use architectural character to provide visual interest, texture and engagement.

### Principles

- P1. Reduce the scale of building mass through vertical or horizontal articulation and using depth in façades.
- P2. Use articulation zones in podiums to reduce mass, provide outdoor space and greenery and create depth and shadow.
- P3. Strive for simplicity of and not complexity in articulation. This includes choosing a simple palette of materials and finishes.
- 4 Articulation zone depth, shadow, greenery

![page 89 img 1 (309x287)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0089-f9afc7de388e.png)


### Controls

- C1. Ensure for articulation of buildings into vertical bays and the integration of landscape into elevations that are seen from public space.
- C2. An articulation zone with a 1m depth should be included in the street wall to allow architectural form to develop. Outdoor space within this zone can be applied to all building uses for amenity, surveillance and to add depth to facades.
- C3. Facades facing the street or public space should be articulated with depth, relief and shadow. A minimum relief of 150mm between the masonry finish and glazing face should be utilised to provide depth and shadow.
- C4. The finishing of service cupboards and basement car park entry should be coordinated in dark recessive colours to minimise the visual impact to the street.

## 4.5 Material and finishes

Buildings in our cities and places need to be composed of low maintenance, robust and quality materials that will last the test of time for sustainability, beauty and to reinforce a sense of place.


### Objectives

- O1. To ensure high-quality materials and finishes are used throughout new development, with an emphasis on the ground floor, to enhance the pedestrian experience.
- O2. To ensure material selection and finishes are robust, have longevity, are low maintenance and contribute to beautiful buildings.
- O3. To ensure new development is compatible with the character and heritage of Punchbowl and Wiley Park.

### Principles

- P1. Primarily use face brickwork, masonry and express the concrete and brick structure on facades.
- P2. Have a higher ratio of solid to void in facades in response to heritage, where appropriate.
- P3. Insert fine detailing through the use of timber, copper and metal.
- P4. Create simplicity through the selection a common language of materials and finishes, rather than selecting many and creating visual complexity.
Image - Articulated and designed brick work frames windows and balconies, Arc, Sydney, NSW (Source: Koichi Takada Architects)


<!-- SRC: 7-7-punchbowl-and-wiley-park.pdf | PAGE: 91 -->

![page 91 img 1 (330x321)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0091-b82177eb3313.png)

![page 91 img 2 (328x325)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0091-18b5d54b5c86.png)


### Controls

- C1. Buildings must include durable single materials such as masonry and face brick. The concrete structure of buildings should form part of the architecture and be expressed in facades.
- C2. Painted cement render or similar painted finishes and Aluminium Composite Panel Cladding, (e.g. Alucobond), should not be used. The use of glazing is not supported for awning construction or for parapet edges on rooftops.
- C3. Elevate the pedestrian experience at street level through the use of textured materials and fine grained detailing using timber, copper and tiles.

## 4.6 Rooftop and podium communal open space


### Objectives

- O1. Ensure that rooftops achieve good amenity standards for residents.
- O2. Encourage the use of rooftops for passive recreation and communal uses.
- O3. Design rooftops to minimise the urban heat island impacts by using landscaping species suitable for windy and dry conditions and by providing shade structures.
- O4. Ensure rooftop open spaces are designed to promote the use of water and energy collected on site.
- O5. Ensure balustrades around rooftop communal spaces are integrated into the design of the space and contributes to the overall appearance.
- O6. Ensure harness anchor points are considered and integrated into the design where required for maintenance works to green roofs and walls.
- O7. Ensure rooftop have amenity for all people.

### Principles

- P1. Include well designed shade structures constructed of low maintenance natural materials for shading to seating areas and for trees and landscape for protection from summer sun and UV.
- P2. Design spaces that people want to linger in due to the provision of shade or winter sun, landscape and facilities for passive socialisation.
Image - Rooftop podium with landscaping and seating, NewLife, Darling Harbour, Ultimo, NSW, by Architectus (Source: Architectus)


<!-- SRC: 7-7-punchbowl-and-wiley-park.pdf | PAGE: 93 -->

![page 93 img 1 (332x594)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0093-33c1984bbbd1.png)


### Controls

- C1. Building rooftops that are designated communal open space areas must be designed to include:
- Fixed seating in areas with shade and solar access, where appropriate;
- Accessible toilet facilities;
- Structures for rain protection and sun shading;
- A BBQ/food preparation area with a sink that is universally accessible;
- Watering systems for proposed landscaping; and
- Stormwater management and disposal.
- C2. Any rooftop structures are to be included in the maximum height of building permitted for the site within CBLEP 2023. The height is to be shown in the Development Application drawings.
- C3. Any proposed communal open space located on the building rooftop is to:
- Be consolidated into a useable area with a minimum width of 6m and a minimum area of 36m².
- Be located so that solar access is provided for users of the open space.
- Be designed to a high quality and allow for landscaping and seating.
- C4. Roof tops are to be structurally sound and have the capacity to support planting and adequate drainage.
- C5. Communal open spaces must be designed to:
- Accommodate both passive and active recreational uses, including clearly defined quiet or passive areas for relaxation and social interaction; and
- Include designated children's play spaces that incorporate age-appropriate features such as swings, play equipment, landscaped mounds, and other interactive elements.
- C6. The functionality, layout, and design quality of communal open spaces must be clearly demonstrated in the submitted architectural and landscape plans.

*Podium with grass and landscaping, Surry Hills Village, NSW by SJB (Source: Architectus)*

## 5.1 Dwelling mix and flexible housing


### Objectives

- O1. Provide a range of housing types and sizes to support diverse households including single person families, multi-generational families, group households, students and seniors.
- O2. Ensure for equitable access to new housing and opportunities for culturally and socioeconomically diverse groups.
- O3. Encourage the design of buildings that are adaptable and flexible to accommodate residents' changing housing needs over their lifetimes.
- O4. Deliver a place-based dwelling mix that suites the needs of the Punchbowl and Wiley Park residents.

### Principles

- P1. Encourage a diversity of housing that meets the needs of the Punchbowl and Wiley Park residents to cater to different social groups.

### Controls

- C1. The following dwelling mix is required for residential flat buildings and shop top housing developments containing 20 or more dwellings:
- Studio: 5-10%.
- 1 bedroom: 10-30%.
- 2 bedroom: 40-75%.
- 3 or more bedroom: minimum 10%.
- C2. The dwelling mix requirements may be altered only if the development serves the purpose of public housing or if the applicant represents a community housing or nonprofit organisation.
- C3. Residential flat buildings should provide accessible apartments for people with a disability and who are elderly and family sized apartments that have level and easy access to adjoining communal space. These apartments should be located at the lower levels of the building to provide ease of access to the street.

*Bellevue Hill Apartments, NSW, Glyde Bautovich (Source: Brett Boardman)*

## 5.2 Parking


### 5.2.1 On-site parking


#### Objectives

- O1. Promote sustainable transport and limit vehicular movements by restricting private parking and facilitating increasing access to, and use of, communal modes of transport within the Precinct.
- O2. Require a lower minimum and maximum parking rate in the Local Village 'Core' near the Punchbowl and Wiley Park Metro stations, with a slightly higher maximum parking rate outside of the Local Village 'Cores' to minimise a reliance on private motor vehicle trips.

#### Principles

- P1. Encourage basement vehicular parking instead of at-grade or above ground parking.
- P2. Provide flexibility for the efficient use of car parking in development by allowing off-site users to use car parking.
- P3. Where provided, design above ground car parking so that it can be adapted to alternate uses over time.
- P4. Consider the location of car park and service vehicle entrances and exits to ensure the amenity of public domain is maintained and improved where possible.
- P5. To facilitate adaptation of car parking to other uses in the long term, above ground car parking is to remain as part of the common property and not part of, or attached to, individual strata units.
Image - Riverside Quay, Southbank, VIC, by Architectus (Source: Architectus).


<!-- SRC: 7-7-punchbowl-and-wiley-park.pdf | PAGE: 97 -->


#### Controls

- C1. All car parking within the Precinct must be provided in accordance with the rates as specified in Table 6 and Figure 49. If a land use is not included in Table 6, the car parking rates in Chapter 3.2 of the CBDCP 2023 will apply.
- C2. Parking for non-residential uses, and nonstaff related parking can be considered collectively and be shared if parking is accessible to the public and the hours of use have different peak demand times.
- C3. If the total Gross Floor Area (GFA) of retail premises exceeds 2,000m², a Transport Impact Assessment for the development proposed is to be prepared and submitted.
- C4. Accessible parking is required to be designed and constructed in accordance with Chapter 3.2-Parking of the CBDCP 2023.

## 5.3 Underground floor space


### Objectives

- O1. To facilitate large floorplate uses underground while maximising activation and permeability at street level.

### Principles

- P1. Uses permitted for underground floor space generally require large floor areas, including neighbourhood supermarkets, larger floorplate retail premises over 1000m² GFA, gym and entertainment facilities.
- P2. Larger sites can accommodate the above mentioned uses as long as it is demonstrated with improved streetscape and public domain impacts.
- P3. The underground uses should not expand beyond the building footprint to ensure that deep soil planting and open space in setback areas are maintained.
- P4. Entries to the underground floor space should have an appropriate, active, ground floor frontage.

## 5.4 Sustainability


### 5.4.1 Urban cooling and environmental sustainability


#### Overview

Urban heat or the Urban heat Island effect refers to the higher temperatures experienced in urban areas compared to rural or natural areas. As more development occurs, the build-up of heat in the environment occurs through heat being trapped in streets, increased hard surfaces, reduced vegetation and heat from air conditioning units.


#### Objectives

- O1. To reduce the contribution of development to urban heat.
- O2. To improve comfort for residents, workers and visitors in the local urban environment.
- O3. To improve the passive comfort of dwellings and reduce the reliance on mechanical systems for amenity.
- O4. To reduce the greenhouse gas emission release to the atmosphere through leakage, or improper disposal, of synthetic refrigerant gases with high Global Warming Potential (GWP).
Image - The Langston Sydney, NSW, by Architectus (Source: Brett Broadman)


#### Controls

- C1. Glazing in the external facade of an enclosed balcony or wintergarden must have a solar absorption of less than 10%.
- C2. Solar absorption of glazing must be marked on plans, and verified through inclusion of window specifications with DA.
- C3. All new air conditioning and refrigeration equipment are to use refrigerants with a GWP of less than 10 if the equipment can be supplied on similar terms to conventional systems. Confirmation prior to the release of the construction certificate is required.
- C4. Solid fuel heating and cooking systems are not permitted in any development.
- C5. Gas cooktops, gas ovens or gas internal space heating systems are not permitted in any residential development. Instead, electric systems must be installed and clearly marked on development application plans.
- C6. Basement carparks must be contained within building footprints and allow for deep soil beneath forecourts and courtyards for large canopy tree planting.
The compliance of a Development Application with the controls in 5.4 is to be shown on the drawings and plans submitted with the Development Application and included in the Statement of Environmental Effects.


<!-- SRC: 7-7-punchbowl-and-wiley-park.pdf | PAGE: 101 -->


### 5.4.2 Reduction of the Urban Heat Island Effect


#### Objectives

- O1. To minimise the reflection of solar heat downward from the building façade into private open space or the public domain.
- O2. To reduce the contribution of development to urban heat and to improve user comfort in the local urban environment.
- O3. To avoid or minimise the impact of heat rejection from air conditioning and refrigeration systems on the urban heat island effect and user comfort in private open space and the public domain.
The compliance of a Development Application with the controls in 5.4 is to be shown on the drawings and plans submitted with the Development Application and included in the Statement of Environmental Effects.


#### Controls

- C1. The extent of the vertical façade of street walls (or if no street wall, as measured from the first 12 metres from the ground plane) that comprise Reflective Surfaces must demonstrate a minimum percentage of shading as defined in Table 7 as calculated at the relevant time of year in Table 9 and Table 10.
- C2. The extent of the vertical façade of the tower (above the street wall or if no street wall, as measured above the first 12 metres from the ground plane) that comprise Reflective Surfaces must demonstrate a minimum percentage of shading as defined in Table 8 as calculated at the relevant time of year in Table 9 and Table 10.
- C3. Compliance with C1 and C2 above is demonstrated on 21 December on the eastfacing façade at 10 AM, northeast and southeast facing façade at 11.30 AM, north-facing façade at 1 PM, northwest and southwest facing façade at 2.30 PM and the west-facing façade at 4 PM as shown in Table 9.
- C4. Compliance with C1 and C2 above is demonstrated on 21 July on the northeastfacing façade at 10 AM, north northeast facing façade at 11.30 AM and 1 PM, and northwest facing façade at 2.30 PM and 4 PM as shown in Table 10.
- C5. Shading may be provided by:
- External feature shading with non-reflective surfaces.
- Intrinsic features of the building form such as reveals and returns.
- Shading from vegetation such as green walls, where requirements for upkeep is covered by a positive covenant.
- C6. Where it is demonstrated that shading cannot be achieved in accordance with C1C4, development must provide:
- A maximum external solar reflectance as defined in Table 8 is required for all Reflective surfaces;
- Applicants must provide elevations illustrating facade surface areas, indicating the location of any shading devices and external finishes, and the solar reflectance value of the cladding;
- Applicants must submit technical information that verifies the solar reflectance value of the cladding; and
- Additional deep soil requirements to offset and reduce urban heat. The additional requirements will be determined by Council on a case by case basis.

Shadows from existing buildings, structures and vegetation are not considered in the calculations. These shadow diagrams are required in addition to, and not instead of, the requisite shadow diagrams to assess solar amenity and compliance with ADG requirements. - Be shaded by a shade structure, or/and;
- Be shaded by a solar panel or/and;
- Be covered by vegetation consistent with the controls on Green Roofs or Walls or/and;
- Provide shading through canopy tree planting, to be measured on the extent of the canopy cover 2 years after planting.
- C9. Where surfaces on rooftops or podiums are not used for private or public open space,

### 5.4.3 Energy efficient (BASIX affected buildings)


#### Objectives

- O1. Promote sustainable development which uses energy efficiently and minimises non-renewable energy usage during the construction and use of buildings.
- O2. Ensure all new developments to actively contribute to the collective effort of reducing energy consumption throughout the Precinct.
- O3. Decrease dependency on the main grid energy supply within the Precinct by implementing alternative energy sources and strategies.

#### Controls

- C1. For developments not covered by BASIX, compliance with the energy efficiency provisions of the Building Code of Australia (Section J) is mandatory. A Section J report, along with annotated plans demonstrating compliance with fabric and service requirements, must be submitted.
- C2. All development not subject to BASIX must issue documentation from a suitably qualified consultant is to be submitted with Development Applications demonstrating the measures that will be used to achieve the relevant energy efficiency scheme rating. Evidence of a formal commitment agreement or registration with the relevant scheme administrator is required to be submitted prior to the issuing of a construction certificate.
- C3. All new developments must future proof the integration of smart technologies for the purposes of monitoring energy usage (e.g. Lighting, heat, ventilation and air conditioning).
- C4. Verification of energy target achievement requires the submission of a signed Commitment Agreement from the National Australian Built Environment Rating System (NABERS).
- C5. Targets for mixed-use developments must be tailored to the specific mix and proportion of land uses, determined on a site-specific basis and at the discretion of the Council.
![page 104 img 1 (380x794)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0104-723d0427eb95.png)


<!-- SRC: 7-7-punchbowl-and-wiley-park.pdf | PAGE: 105 -->


### 5.4.4 Water efficiency


#### Objectives

- O1. Reduce the consumption of drinking water.
- O2. Increase the amount of water harvested from rainwater and urban stormwater runoff for use.
- O3. Increase resilience to the impacts of water scarcity by providing sustainable alternative water supplies.
- O4. Decrease the technical and financial barriers to retrospective upgrades to buildings to connect to future non drinking water supply infrastructure.

#### Controls

- C1. All new developments must include submetering and future proof for smart technologies to minimise water consumption.
- C2. Cooling towers must be designed in accordance with best practice guidelines to reduce water consumption.
- C3. All development not subject to BASIX will need to incorporate the following watersaving measures:
- Plumbing fixtures are to meet minimum Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards (WELS) Scheme Standards including 4 star rated showerheads, 4 star rated toilet cisterns, 5 star rated urinals and 6 star rated water tap outlets.
- Appliances (dishwashers, clothes washers etc) are to be 5 stars (WELS Scheme) or better rated for water use efficiency.
- C4. All development not subject to BASIX must issue documentation from a suitably qualified consultant is to be submitted with development Applications demonstrating the measures that will be used to achieve the relevant water efficiency scheme rating. Evidence of a formal commitment agreement or registration with the relevant scheme administrator is required to be submitted prior to the issuing of a construction certificate.
- C5. Verification of energy target achievement requires the submission of a signed Commitment Agreement from the National Australian Built Environment Rating System (NABERS).
- C6. Targets for mixed-use developments must be tailored to the specific mix and proportion of land uses, determined on a site-specific basis and at the discretion of the Council.

<!-- SRC: 7-7-punchbowl-and-wiley-park.pdf | PAGE: 106 -->


### 5.4.5 Electric Buildings


#### Objectives

- O1. To minimise the reliance on the consumption of fossil fuels in new development.
- O2. To prevent indoor pollutants associated with combustion.

#### Controls

- C1. All new mixed-use development, residential development, commercial premises, tourist and visitor accommodation, health services facilities and educational establishments are to use only electricity for all energy requirements associated with normal operations.
- C2. The use of fossil fuels for any purpose is not to exceed 1% of the projected annual energy demand for the building. **
* Note: BASIX certification for residential developments at a DA stage must not rely on gas for heating or hot water to comply with Control C1.

** Note: This control excludes emergency services and emergency infrastructure such as pumps and generators utilised in the case of emergencies (flood, fire, etc). 1% of projected annual energy demand for fossil fuels allows for the use of diesel for standby generation.

![page 106 img 1 (735x796)](images/canterbury-bankstown-development-control-plan-2023/p0106-07e4e410fc00.png)


<!-- SRC: 7-7-punchbowl-and-wiley-park.pdf | PAGE: 107 -->


### 5.4.6 Solar energy requirements


#### Objectives

- O1. Maximise the on-site collection of renewable energy.
- O2. Minimise the consumption of electricity generated from non-renewable resources.

#### Controls

- C1. Development must include the installation of a solar PV system of no less capacity than:
- For sites with multiple electricity meters; rooftop photovoltaic (solar) panel system is connected to the common meter and the system is sized to offset 90-100% of estimated base building maximum demand.
- For sites with a central electricity meter; the rooftop photovoltaic (solar) panels systems is sized to offset 30% of estimated maximum demand.
- C2. With any DA plans submitted, the roof plan must show the area(s) allocated to PVs and necessary access requirements for cleaning and routine maintenance. PV solar panels must be setback at least 2m from the edge of the build roof or parapet.

## 6.1 Key sites overview

The following sites have been identified as having a pivotal role in the realisation of the vision and objectives for the Punchbowl and Wiley Park Precinct.

The key sites will be a catalyst for development of the Precinct and present an opportunity for examples of design excellence, an integrated response to Connection with Country principles and the reflection of Punchbowl and Wiley Parks history and heritage through building form and materiality. The development on key sites will share a common language that is place based.

To ensure for optimal outcomes for Punchbowl and Wiley Park and an efficient process for applicants, it is essential to engage with Council early in the Development Application process. Council will have an expectation to see detailed analysis of the site, the context and an understanding of the Aboriginal and European history of Punchbowl and Wiley Park.

To ensure for a 'fine grained' approach to key sites, Council encourages the subdivision of large sites into smaller lots that are contextual to the site. If this cannot be achieved, then a variety of different buildings should be introduced of varying architectural character, scale and height to provide individual identity for residents and visitors.


### Objectives

- O1. Ensure that development is unique to the character, climate and demography of the Punchbowl and Wiley Park Precinct.
- O2. To achieve Design Excellence by creating inspirational key sites with high quality innovative architecture that are sustainably built, reference history and heritage, offer community benefit and provide new publicly accessible and private spaces that contribute positively to the Precincts sense of place.
- O3. Ensure that the principles of Connecting with Country are intrinsically represented in these sites.
- O4. Ensure development does not compromise or reduce solar access to parks.
- O5. Integrate shared lanes and pedestrian links, expand the public domain, improve pedestrian and cyclist permeability and connect to existing and new open space.
- O6. Provide for a range of heights on key sites to create an interesting and diverse skyline.
- O7. Ensure that the interface of these larger sites activates the public domain and invites the public into new publicly accessible spaces.
- O8. Ensure that podiums are articulated to appear as smaller parts to create a positive fine grained and exciting experiences at street level.
- O9. Ensure street blocks present as a group of buildings and not as a single building.
- O10. Ensure for a common language between older buildings and new development by using existing materials that are characteristic in the Precinct. These materials are long lasting and need little maintenance such as masonry, face brick and natural building materials generally.
- O11. Integrate landscape as an key part of the building form, open space and the development generally. Extend tree canopy and deep soil and provide for green cover to reduce urban heat gain.
